findings.title: Findings converge on the cross-tree pairing mechanism (matching kinds, predicate, and tie-break order)
findings.why_it_matters: Four findings from both critics land on one mechanism: how a head finding is paired with a base finding. D5 pairs on equality, D6 pairs on containment, D10 adds a catalog field to route between the kinds, and both D5 and D6 use a rename-mapped "same file first, then any file" tie-break. The Senior Engineer shows the tie-break order is unspecified and can blame an untouched file (Finding 4). The Minimalist argues that equality and containment are one algorithm with two predicates (Finding 6), that the catalog field then has one consumer (Finding 7), and that the run-wide rename map exists only to break ties (Finding 8). Each proposes its own patch: a two-pass order, a merged predicate, a deleted field, a scoped rename map. Is the pairing mechanism itself under-specified, so it should be re-evaluated as a whole (how many matching kinds, what predicate, what deterministic pairing order, whether path preference uses the rename map at all, whether the routing needs a catalog field), rather than patched four times?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the pairing mechanism before addressing the converging findings individually.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the pairing mechanism before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: how many matching kinds are needed; whether the predicate is equality, containment, or equality first and then containment; what deterministic order pairs findings (per-finding greedy, per-pass, or maximum matching); whether same-file preference needs the rename map; and whether routing needs a catalog field or a branch.
findings.choice_reason: Settled: pass-based pairing, exact before containment, run-wide rename map and base_match kept

findings.title: Findings converge on HSL102's line-count source (D7 reading the extractions outside the scan)
findings.why_it_matters: D7 counts head and base lines by reading files from the extractions after the scans, using the rename map to find the base path and counting 0 when the path is missing. Three findings from both critics land on this one mechanism. It is a second read outside `load_file` on a path discovery never vetted (Finding 9). Its "count 0" infers the base state, which can disagree with what the base scan saw: a file excluded, decode-failed, or pragma-suppressed at base (Finding 10). And the base scan already knows whether the base file was over the threshold (Finding 7). Both critics independently propose taking the base side from the base scan instead. Should D7's line-count source be re-evaluated (whether extraction reads are needed at all, what an unreadable or excluded base file means, whether HSL102 needs a catalog hook) before patching each finding?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate HSL102's line-count source before addressing the converging findings individually.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate HSL102's line-count source before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: whether reading the extractions is needed at all; what an unreadable, excluded, or suppressed base file means for the ratchet; whether HSL102 needs a catalog hook.
findings.choice_reason: Settled: base scan decides; counts round-trip through file_length.py's own message

findings.title: The design never says the head config comes from the HEAD extraction, or how it is resolved there
findings.why_it_matters: D4 says "the head tree's config" and step 2 says "the working tree is never read". Today the only path is `cli.check` → `resolve_project(root, config)` from the cwd → `load_config`, which reads the working tree. Run unchanged, an uncommitted `max_lines` or `select` edit changes the gate for the committed code. That is flaw 2 again, this time for config. The design maps the root (line 30) and an explicit `--config` (line 112) into each extraction, but doesn't say how the config is found inside the extraction or what happens when the HEAD commit has no config at that path (for example, a config file that exists only uncommitted). If resolution inside the extraction ever runs without an explicit root, `resolve_project` walks up past the extraction (discovery.py:547-556). It stops only at a `.git` entry, which an extraction lacks, so a stray `/tmp/pyproject.toml` could apply. Line 30 implies an explicit root, which avoids that walk, but the design doesn't say so.
findings.chosen: A: Say in D4 that `new_code` resolves the root and config in the working tree only to get their repo-relative paths, then loads the config from the same path in the HEAD extraction with an explicit root (no upward discovery). With no config at that path in HEAD, the run uses the default config, as a normal run with no config does.
findings.recommended: A: Say in D4 that `new_code` resolves the root and config in the working tree only to get their repo-relative paths, then loads the config from the same path in the HEAD extraction with an explicit root (no upward discovery). With no config at that path in HEAD, the run uses the default config, as a normal run with no config does.

findings.title: D6's containment pairing order is unspecified and greedy, so the finding reported as new can land on an old, untouched occurrence
findings.why_it_matters: Containment is symmetric and not transitive, so one short occurrence can pair with many base occurrences. D5's wording (line 137) is per head finding: try the same file, then any file. D6's wording ("same file first, then any file, one to one") is ambiguous between that and two passes. Under the per-finding reading, take a base with copies A and B (200 lines each) and a PR that adds a short copy X in file C whose text is inside A. If X is visited first, it takes base-A through the any-file fallback. Head-A then falls back to base-B, and head-B is left over and reported as new. The count is right, but the CI annotation points at untouched file B and X goes unreported. Running the same-file pass over all findings before the any-file pass avoids this case. The design doesn't say which it does.
findings.recommended: A: Specify pass-based pairing in D5 and D6: equality first (same file, then any file), then containment for the rest, with ties broken by smallest length difference and then path. Add a test for the long-plus-short case.

findings.title: `git diff -M` warnings on large PRs fail the gate through `run_git`'s "any stderr is failure" rule
findings.why_it_matters: `run_git` raises `GitFailure` on any non-empty stderr, even with exit 0 (discovery.py:158-173). When rename candidates exceed `diff.renameLimit`, git prints `warning: exhaustive rename detection was skipped due to too many files` to stderr. Reusing `run_git`, the natural reuse, turns a large move or split PR into a hard error, and that is the PR HSL102 pushes people to make. The rename output also depends on user config (`diff.renames`, `diff.renameLimit`, `core.quotepath`) unless the flags are pinned, and without `-z` git quotes non-ASCII names. A rename below git's 50% similarity default gets base count 0, so it is reported as new growth, and the design doesn't say whether that's accepted.
findings.chosen: A: Specify `git diff -z --name-status -M -l0` through `run_git` in D7. State that a rename below the similarity threshold counts as a new file (base 0).
findings.recommended: A: Specify `git diff -z --name-status -M -l0` through `run_git` in D7. State that a rename below the similarity threshold counts as a new file (base 0).

findings.title: HSL104 containment could fold into the generic matcher, leaving HSL102 the only special case
findings.why_it_matters: D5 (equality on whitespace-free span text) and D6 (containment on the same text) are the same pairing over the same inputs with a different predicate. A single matcher using "equal or one contains the other" would need no HSL104 hook. The real difference is the message: HSL104's message counts places (`duplicated code of N lines in K places`, duplicate_code.py:161), so it changes whenever a copy is added, and the key would have to drop or normalise the message for HSL104. The cost is a looser D5. Containment for every rule passes edits that extend a flagged span (`X=1` → `X=10` for HSL004), and lets a short new finding match a longer old one elsewhere, for example a new `# TODO` comment inside an old `# TODO: fix later`. That reverses D5's ratified "touching it re-reports it" row.
findings.recommended: B: Keep separate equality and containment kinds, as ratified.

findings.title: HSL102 may not need a catalog hook or extraction counting; the base scan's own HSL102 finding answers most cases
findings.why_it_matters: Under D4 both runs use the head config, so if the base scan has no HSL102 finding at the mapped path, the base file was at or under the threshold, the head is over it, and the finding is new. Only when both have a finding is a count comparison needed. That removes the "count 0 for a new file" special case and most of the extraction reads. If Finding 6 is also applied, `base_match` (D10) has one consumer and could be a branch. The catch: when both findings exist, the base count has to come from somewhere, either the message (which D7's deciding factor rejects) or a read.
findings.recommended: A: Derive "new" from the base scan's HSL102 finding, and read line counts only when both trees have one.

findings.title: The rename map is run-wide machinery that only D7 strictly needs
findings.why_it_matters: Step 1 computes the rename map for every run, and D5 and D6 use it only to prefer the same file when several identically keyed findings tie. For D5's equality key, the count of new findings per key is max(0, head − base) whatever the pairing, so the map changes only which finding is cited. D7 can't work without it. Dropping it from D5 and D6 makes the matcher take only findings and text, with no path translation. The counterpoint is Finding 4: which finding is cited is what CI annotations show, and for D6's containment, pairing order can matter beyond the citation.

findings.title: D7 reads files a second time outside `load_file`, on a base path discovery never vetted
findings.why_it_matters: CLAUDE.md requires each scanned file to be read once through `source.load_file`, and discovery's containment check vets symlinks. D7 reads head and base files "directly" to count lines. A base path from the rename map never went through discovery, so a tracked symlink at base pointing outside the extraction would be followed. The count must also match the detector's decoding (BOM, encoding cookie), and a separate read risks a second decoding implementation that drifts. The cache-coherence reason behind the CLAUDE.md rule matters less here, since the extraction is private and nothing edits it mid-run. The symlink and decoding concerns remain.
findings.recommended: A: Say in D7 that counts come from the scans, or from `load_file` and `parse_python` on a contained path, never a raw read.

findings.title: HSL102's base state is inferred from the extraction and can disagree with the base scan
findings.why_it_matters: "Count 0 when the file didn't exist at base" is inferred from the rename map and the base extraction. If the base file exists but failed to decode or parse, was excluded, or carried `ignore-file HSL102`, the extraction path and the base scan disagree, and D7 doesn't say which wins. `file_length.detect` uses `source.text`, which exists only for a parsed file, so a base file that didn't decode has no count from the detector's path. Counting it as 0 makes every head HSL102 finding for it look like growth.
findings.recommended: A: State in D7 that a base file without a count counts as 0, so its head HSL102 finding is new. It matches "a file added with too many lines counts as growing from 0".

findings.title: The cache location type may be a bigger refactor than splitting the flag needs
findings.why_it_matters: The need is to scan an extraction while using the real root's default cache, with the managed-default treatment (self-ignore marker and symlink check). Today `run_scan` derives both from `cache_dir is None` (pipeline.py:204, 227), and `prepare_cache_dir` already takes `self_ignore` as a keyword (cache.py:442). The design replaces `cache_dir: Path | None` with a location type through `RunCache` and `cache.py`. The Minimalist suggests two explicit keyword parameters on `run_scan` (`cache_base`, plus a caller-decided managed flag) instead. The critic overstates one point: a one-parameter fix isn't enough, because passing the default path as an explicit `cache_dir` loses the symlink check. Two values are needed either way, so the choice is between a small type and two parameters.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the location type, but stop it at `run_scan` and `RunCache`. `cache.py`'s functions keep their explicit `self_ignore` bool.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the location type, but stop it at `run_scan` and `RunCache`. `cache.py`'s functions keep their explicit `self_ignore` bool.

findings.title: D5's "swap" row overstates what it catches: a swap with identical text passes
findings.why_it_matters: The D5 table says that fixing one lazy import and adding a different one in the same file is reported as New. The key is rule, message, and whitespace-free span text, with no path. So when the removed and added findings have the same text (HSL002 `import json` in `f()` fixed, `import json` added in `g()`, or in another file), they match and the swap passes. The debt moves. That follows from the ratified "moves pass" stance, but the table row reads as though swaps are always caught.
findings.chosen: A: Reword the D5 swap row to separate different-text swaps (New) from identical-text swaps (pass).
findings.recommended: A: Reword the D5 swap row to separate different-text swaps (New) from identical-text swaps (pass).

findings.title: Skip the base extraction and scan when the head run has no findings
findings.why_it_matters: With zero head findings there's nothing to subtract, so the merge-base lookup, the base extraction, and the base scan can all be skipped. That halves the cost of a clean run, house-lint linting itself for example. It does nothing for a backlog repo like hassette. It also changes behaviour slightly: a base-only scan error, which Posture says fails the run, would no longer be seen.

findings.title: A base-only scan error fails the PR that fixes it
findings.why_it_matters: Posture says an error from either run fails the gate. A parse or decode failure, or a jscpd failure, that exists only at the merge-base therefore fails a PR whose purpose is to fix it. Parse failures are error results (scanner.py:57, 91). This is raised once, against a ratified posture.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a scan error present only at the merge-base fails the gate, so the PR fixing it has to merge without the gate.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a scan error present only at the merge-base fails the gate, so the PR fixing it has to merge without the gate.

findings.title: Extraction depends on git environment and checkout state the design doesn't pin
findings.why_it_matters: `run_git` inherits the environment on purpose (discovery.py:158-162). Inside hooks, `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_INDEX_FILE` or `GIT_WORK_TREE` may be set, and the design overrides only `GIT_INDEX_FILE` for `read-tree`. The critic also raises sparse checkouts (skip-worktree bits making `checkout-index` skip files) and blobless clones (blob fetches mid-run). Nothing checks that an extraction is complete, so a silent partial extraction would make findings vanish from both trees, against Posture's "fail loudly". The sparse-checkout mechanism is unverified: a fresh temporary index from a plain `read-tree` may not carry skip-worktree bits at all.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: extraction assumes a full, non-sparse clone and an ordinary hook environment.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: extraction assumes a full, non-sparse clone and an ordinary hook environment.

findings.title: Temporary extractions leak on SIGKILL or timeout and copy every tracked file
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: larger repos than hassette. "Always removed" holds for exceptions, not for SIGKILL, a CI timeout, or an interrupted hook. Each leaked directory is a full copy of every tracked file, binary assets included, though only configured languages are scanned.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a killed run can leave its temporary extractions in the system temp directory.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a killed run can leave its temporary extractions in the system temp directory.

findings.title: The `--base` ref is passed to git without verification
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: CI where the ref name isn't controlled by the maintainer. The design never says the ref is protected from being read as an option, so a value starting with `-` would be. Git refnames can't start with `-`, so `github.base_ref` can't trigger it. The input is the user's own CLI argument.
findings.chosen: A: Resolve the ref with `rev-parse --verify --end-of-options <ref>^{commit}` before any other git call, and use the SHA from then on.
findings.recommended: A: Resolve the ref with `rev-parse --verify --end-of-options <ref>^{commit}` before any other git call, and use the SHA from then on.
